name: Breast forms

lead: Breast forms are prosthetic breasts, most often made of silicone or water-based gel in a plastic film so they feel like skin. They are used after mastectomy or lumpectomy, by many trans women and crossdressers before or without hormone therapy, and for aesthetic reasons. They give an immediate breast shape and symmetry under clothing.

The main body of research concerns women after mastectomy: trials in Giessen, Germany, found that self-adhesive forms improved scores on social contact and body acceptance compared with standard bra-worn forms.

paras: Forms come in full shapes that sit on the chest wall, partial shapes worn over remaining tissue, shells that fit over a smaller breast, stick-on versions, and custom-made forms matched for colour, size and contour. Bra-worn forms sit in a pocket or cup; adhesive forms stick to the skin and can be worn under a regular bra. Silicone forms are usually weighted to feel like natural breast tissue, and are cleaned like skin with soap and water.

Reported problems are practical: about half of patients in one adhesive-form study had trouble with adhesiveness, and hot flushes can affect adhesion. Silicone can be punctured by pins or brooches and damaged by chlorine or salt water if not rinsed.

angle.text: A form adds breast volume and shape immediately and can be removed. After mastectomy it restores symmetry; for others it creates a breast shape without surgery or hormones.

lead: Breast prostheses, or breast forms, are shapes that look and often feel like breasts. They are used after mastectomy or lumpectomy, before feminizing hormone therapy, and for aesthetic reasons [1]. The most common construction is a silicone or water-based gel in a plastic film designed to feel like skin [1].

For appearance they provide an instant chest silhouette and, for people who have lost breast tissue on one side, balance and symmetry. Wikipedia notes that tissue removal can affect balance and posture and that a prosthesis may help correct this and ease loss of self-esteem [1]. Many pre- or non-hormonal trans women, crossdressers and some nonbinary people also use them [1].

Clinical research is mostly on mastectomy patients. A 1995 randomized trial of 67 women compared custom bra-worn forms with self-adhesive forms and found significant differences in the Social Contact and Relations scale, with most patients preferring the self-adhesive type [2][3].

paras: Full or standard forms sit on the chest wall after all breast tissue has been removed and can be customized for size, shape and skin tone. Partial forms use two silicone layers worn over remaining tissue inside the bra, and shells fit over a smaller breast to match a larger one [1]. Stick-on versions adhere to the skin, and custom-made forms are tailored in silicone or latex [1].

Shapes differ: asymmetric forms extend toward the armpit to mimic the tail of Spence, while symmetric triangle or teardrop forms do not. Silicone forms are typically weighted to match natural breasts, and lighter versions are about 20 to 40 percent lighter [1]. A 1989 US patent describes a form held in a pocket attached to a bra cup, with a weighted member in an internal chamber [4].

Frederick Cox received a US patent in 1874 for an air-filled rubber breast pad, and Charles Morehouse patented an inflatable natural-rubber version in 1885 [1]. In 1904 Laura Wolfe's design replaced air with down feather and silk floss filling [1]. In the mid-twentieth century development expanded and marketing grew beyond post-surgical use [1].

Mastectomy is the most common use, whether temporary, long term or as a stand-in before reconstruction; insurance may require a prescription. Mastectomy bras have pockets to hold the form, and homemade fillers such as shoulder pads are also used [1]. After lumpectomy, partial or attachable forms fill missing tissue [1].
Trans women and crossdressers use forms to create a breast shape, and full-frontal cleavage tops are marketed to this group, though the neck edge can be visible [1].
Silicone is treated like skin: washed daily with soap and water, dried thoroughly and rinsed after swimming to avoid chlorine or salt damage. Pins and brooches can puncture it [1].

In a 1995 trial in Giessen, 67 women after unilateral mastectomy were randomized to custom bra-worn forms or self-adhesive forms. After 3 months there were significant differences on the Social Contact and Relations scale; most were better satisfied with the self-adhesive type, found their weight and movement natural, and 78 percent could wear more fashionable clothing [2][3].

A 1998 follow-up of 55 patients over about six months found significant differences on scales including self-acceptance of the body and acceptance of the body by others, but about half had adhesion problems; those with smooth, flat scars and no hot flushes were more likely to benefit [5].

An earlier Australian survey of 49 women found only 44 percent had been able to choose their prosthesis and 28 percent were dissatisfied; the authors stated that an appropriate prosthesis can reduce the sense of disfigurement [6].
